mechanism: A hosted agent takes one natural-language prompt, splits it into sub-tasks, runs several of them in parallel in a cloud sandbox, and returns a generated app such as a CRM or dashboard with a database and front end. The moving parts are an LLM planner, code-writing workers, a managed runtime and a hosting step. The quality depends on the planner's decomposition and on whatever data connectors the prompt names.
claim: One prompt builds a working CRM or dashboard, with tasks running in parallel.
why_not_testable: The hosted product needs an account and credits, and the promo gives no specific claim to check.
needs: An account on the vendor's agent product.
one_line: A one-prompt CRM and dashboard builder runs sub-tasks in parallel; the idea is the same fan-out Claude Code sub-agents already do.
idea_why: Parallel decomposition of a build prompt is sound, but whether the output beats a Claude Code build is an empirical question nobody has run.
breakdown: Write one brief for a small CRM (contacts, pipeline stages, a dashboard of counts). Have a parent Claude Code session split it into schema, API, UI and seed-data tasks and run them as parallel sub-agents in separate folders. Wire the pieces with a single SQLite file and a static front end. Time it and count manual fixes, then compare to the vendor's own demo output if someone with an account runs it. A hired person would only be needed to judge whether the result is usable by a real client.

mechanism: A Claude Code plugin registers hooks on tool calls, model steps, skills and subagents. Each hook event is classified into a station (files, shell, network and so on) by reading the tool name and, for shell, the command's first word, then pushed to a pane that animates pulses. Worn spokes and a route line are just counters and a short history of the last stations.
claim: A live local map beside the chat showing what Claude Code is doing, with refusals and errors in red.
verdict_question: Does the repo's command-to-station classifier put the README's own examples (cat, grep, curl, git push, python -c) in the stations the README says, out of 10 checked?
probe_title: lot-map: does its shell-command classifier assign README example commands to the stations the README claims?
one_line: lot-map turns Claude Code hook events into a live pulse map, classifying shell commands by their first word, which it admits misses python -c network calls.
idea_why: Hooks already carry the tool name and input, so a station map is a cheap and honest view of where agent work goes.

mechanism: An agent follows a written procedure on a few runs while logging its tool calls and the reason it gives for each. A model reads those logs to extract the condition behind each step, merges conditions across runs into a rule document, and generates an executable workflow where plain code picks the next step. Failures on training runs are fed back for repair rounds.
claim: Distilled workflows reach 93.8 percent completion versus 96.8 percent for the agent at 24 percent lower cost, and run in 1.3s instead of 170s on tau2-Bench.
why_not_testable: The method needs model calls and the authors' production procedures, and there is no local LLM.
needs: Model API calls and a set of logged agent runs.
one_line: ReTrace compiles a few logged agent runs into plain code that picks the next step, cutting a 170 second task to 1.3 seconds for a small accuracy loss.
idea_why: Turning repeated agent behaviour into deterministic code is how repeated jobs get cheap, and the repair loop is a known pattern.
breakdown: Pick one repeated Proteus nightly step that a sub-agent currently drives. Log three runs with the stated reason for each tool call. Ask a model to write the if-then rules behind each step, merge them, and generate a small Python script. Run the script against held-out nights and count agreements with the agent. A person is only needed to review the rules for errors.

mechanism: A short-form post opens with a pain the target group recognises, then lists five concrete outcomes as bullets, then points to a paid community. The structure works by qualifying the audience in the first line and making the offer scannable. The numbers come from comments, follows and sign-ups from that post, measured against a similar post without the structure.
claim: A pain-first hook with a five-bullet outcome list sells a niche community.
why_not_testable: A test needs a live audience and a posting account, which cannot be run keyless in a sandbox.
needs: An audience and a posting account.
one_line: Pain-first hook plus five outcome bullets is a template for niche community posts; its effect is untested without an audience.
idea_why: The structure is common copywriting, but whether it beats other openers for a given niche needs a split test.
breakdown: Write two versions of the same post, one pain-first with five bullets and one plain description. Post both to the same audience on different days and record comments, clicks and joins per thousand views. The copy can be drafted with Claude Code and the outbound-email skill's rules, but a person must post and approve it. Compare after a fixed window.

mechanism: The game's compiled machine code is translated ahead of time into native ARM64 code, with the old console-style system calls and graphics calls mapped to macOS equivalents such as Metal. A coding agent wrote the lifting and glue code, and the user supplies their own game files from Steam. Nothing is emulated at run time, which is why speed is close to native.
claim: Black Ops II runs at about 60fps on a Mac with no emulator, by static recompilation.
why_not_testable: It needs a licensed copy of the game and an Apple Silicon Mac, and this is an Intel Mac.
needs: A Steam copy of the game and an ARM64 Mac.
one_line: A Mac port of Black Ops II built by static recompilation with an AI agent, with no emulator and about 60fps.
idea_why: Static recompilation is a proven technique, but how much of the work the agent really did is unclear from the post.
breakdown: Start with a tiny binary, disassemble it with an open tool, lift instructions to an intermediate form and emit ARM64. Map each system and graphics call to a shim and test against known outputs. A real game needs a person to resolve the many ambiguous cases and to settle licensing, since only the user's own copy may be converted.

mechanism: A set of hooks runs on each user message, before a command and after an error, looks up short recipe files called atoms in a local folder, and injects the best matches into the agent's context. Lookup is by words, optionally by a local embedding model. Agents write new atoms as they work, in a fixed spec, so the base grows with use.
claim: Hooks make Claude Code, Codex and others recall and record what worked, so they stop re-solving the same problem.

idea_why: Surfacing a checked recipe on an error is the same idea as a memory index, applied at hook time.

mechanism: A student model is trained with reinforcement learning in five long-horizon environments where it uses ordinary bash and files as its memory across context resets. A frozen teacher that already knows file operations gives token-level guidance via on-policy distillation. The training runs asynchronously across all environments with one shared policy.
claim: CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest on-policy distillation baseline and transfers to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2.
why_not_testable: It needs GPU training of a language model, which this Mac cannot do.
one_line: Agents can learn to use plain files as long-term memory when the teacher already knows file tools; a trained student gains 2.97 times the baseline.
idea_why: Using ordinary files as memory fits what models already know, which matches how Claude Code memory folders work today.
breakdown: The training itself is out of reach here. The usable part is the design lesson: give an agent a persistent workspace and ordinary file tools rather than special memory tools. Proteus already does this with its memory folder, so the practical step is to log how often runs read and write it. A person would be needed only to run training on rented hardware.
tools_have: Claude Code with skills and sub-agents
missing: GPU training capacity and the CAMG-II environments.

mechanism: A post asks viewers to comment a keyword. A third-party automation service watches the post's comments through the platform's business messaging API and sends each commenter an automatic direct message with a link. It raises engagement counts and builds a contact list. Platforms limit this with API rate limits, requiring a business account and a prior comment, and they flag accounts that send repetitive messages or inflate comments.
claim: Comment a keyword and get the link by DM.
why_not_testable: It needs a social account and the platform's messaging API, and the vault says understand only, never operate.
needs: A business social account and an automation service subscription.
one_line: Comment-for-DM funnels use a keyword trigger and an auto-reply API; platforms limit them by rate caps and flag repetitive messaging.
idea_why: As a lead-capture trigger it is legitimate when the commenter asked for the link, but it is easily abused for engagement inflation.
breakdown: Understand it only. Read the platform's public documentation for private replies to comments and note the limits: one private reply per comment, a short window, and a business account. Record what the platform says about spam and repeated messaging. No operation is planned. A person would be needed for any real account setup.
